system:
You are an art-world editor compiling a gallery guide for Seattle, . Answer with the
JSON object the schema describes and nothing else. Rank by significance and influence in the
contemporary art world: programme quality, the artists represented, art-fair presence, critical and
institutional attention, and longevity. Include commercial galleries and the nonprofit, artist-run and
project spaces that show contemporary art to the public in Seattle itself (galleries whose home is
elsewhere count only through a permanent Seattle space). Exclude museums, art fairs, auction houses,
framers, art schools, decor shops, online-only dealers and advisories. For every gallery give its usual
name; its official website when you are confident of it, else null; the district it is in, using one of
these labels when it fits (Pioneer Square, Downtown, Capitol Hill, Ballard/Fremont, Georgetown, University District) else the district name you know; a street address hint when you
know it (street and number are enough), else null; its kind (gallery, museum, nonprofit, project_space, university, other); and a short note on why it
matters. Every entry must be a distinct venue — list a gallery with several Seattle spaces once.
user: What are the 100 most significant and influential galleries in Seattle, ranked in order? If less than 100 significant galleries exist, provide the complete list of significant galleries.

galleries.name: Greg Kucera Gallery
galleries.note: Seattle's flagship contemporary dealer since 1983; museum-quality shows, a deep print program and the region's most consistent art-fair and institutional presence.

galleries.name: Traver Gallery
galleries.note: Founded 1977; the gallery that made Northwest studio glass an international story, now balancing glass with painting and sculpture, with long-running fair participation.

galleries.name: Winston Wächter Fine Art
galleries.note: Seattle–New York dealer with a polished contemporary painting and photography roster and steady Art Miami / Seattle Art Fair presence.

galleries.name: Foster/White Gallery
galleries.note: Operating since 1968, one of the oldest and largest commercial spaces in the city; bridges Northwest School legacies with mid-career contemporary artists.

galleries.name: Wa Na Wari
galleries.note: Black art space in a family home in the Central District; nationally covered model for art, anti-displacement work and community archive.

galleries.name: ARTS at King Street Station
galleries.note: City-run cultural space whose top-floor gallery opened with yəhaw̓; the largest publicly programmed contemporary exhibition hall outside the museums.

galleries.name: MadArt Studio
galleries.note: Commissions large-scale installations built on site in public view; has given ambitious platforms to artists such as John Grade and Lauren Iida.

galleries.name: SOIL Gallery
galleries.note: Artist-run cooperative founded 1995 and the incubator for a generation of Seattle artists; still the city's most credible experimental co-op.

galleries.name: Davidson Galleries
galleries.note: Since 1974 the Northwest's authority on works on paper, pairing antique master prints with a serious contemporary print and drawing program.

galleries.name: Linda Hodges Gallery
galleries.note: Thirty-plus years of representational and narrative painting; a core stop on the First Thursday circuit and a steady supporter of regional mid-career artists.

galleries.name: J. Rinehart Gallery
galleries.note: The most energetic newer commercial gallery in Pioneer Square, with a diverse emerging roster and strong Seattle Art Fair visibility.

galleries.name: James Harris Gallery
galleries.note: For two decades Seattle's most internationally connected program (Bunny Rogers, Claude Zervas, Robert Yoder) before closing its space in 2021; still the benchmark local dealers are measured against.

galleries.name: studio e
galleries.note: Dawna Holloway's compact Georgetown room with an outsized critical reputation for tightly curated shows by respected Northwest artists.

galleries.name: Koplin Del Rio
galleries.note: Long-established Los Angeles gallery that relocated to Seattle in 2017 and later joined forces with Prographica; figurative work and drawing of national standing.

galleries.name: Jacob Lawrence Gallery
galleries.address_hint: UW School of Art, 15th Ave NE
galleries.note: University of Washington's kunsthalle-style gallery; adventurous curated projects, visiting-artist shows and a link to the Jacob Lawrence legacy.

galleries.name: Gallery 4Culture
galleries.note: King County's juried exhibition space; a career-launching solo slot for emerging and mid-career artists, free of commercial pressure.

galleries.name: Stonington Gallery
galleries.note: Leading dealer of contemporary Northwest Coast and Alaska Native art since 1979, with artists collected by major museums.

galleries.name: Photographic Center Northwest
galleries.note: The region's photography hub; its gallery brings national photographers and juried surveys to Seattle audiences.

galleries.name: Method Gallery
galleries.note: Single-installation white box devoted to site-responsive sculpture and immersive projects — a rare non-commercial platform for ambitious three-dimensional work.

galleries.name: Punch Gallery
galleries.note: Artist-run collective since 2007 known for conceptually driven solo shows and invitational projects.

galleries.name: Gallery110
galleries.note: Long-running artist cooperative with a juried associate program; a dependable entry point for emerging Seattle artists.

galleries.name: Abmeyer + Wood Fine Art
galleries.note: Downtown gallery of contemporary sculpture, glass and painting with an international roster and consistent presence at major fairs.

galleries.name: Steinbrueck Native Gallery
galleries.note: Major Waterfront dealer in contemporary Northwest Coast Native art, representing established carvers, printmakers and weavers.

galleries.name: ArtXchange Gallery
galleries.note: Globally oriented program of diaspora and immigrant artists; socially engaged exhibitions with a strong community education component.

galleries.name: Bryan Ohno Gallery
galleries.note: Contemporary Japanese and Asian-American art, including projects with Gerard Tsutakawa; long history of ambitious sculptural exhibitions.

galleries.name: Harris Harvey Gallery
galleries.note: Specialist in contemporary and historic Northwest painting near Pike Place; scholarly presentation of the regional canon.

galleries.name: Lisa Harris Gallery
galleries.note: In Pike Place Market since 1985, showing Northwest landscape and figurative painters with an unusually loyal collector base.

galleries.name: Patricia Rovzar Gallery
galleries.note: Thirty-year-old downtown gallery of contemporary Northwest painting and mixed media, active in corporate and civic collections.

galleries.name: Woodside/Braseth Gallery
galleries.note: Founded 1962 and Seattle's oldest continuously operating gallery; custodian of the Northwest School and its contemporary descendants.

galleries.name: Gallery IMA
galleries.note: Long-running Pioneer Square gallery mixing contemporary painting, sculpture and craft-based media.

galleries.name: Center on Contemporary Art (CoCA)
galleries.note: Founded 1980, Seattle's veteran alternative art organization; historically the venue for the city's most provocative exhibitions and performances.

galleries.name: Vermillion Art Gallery and Bar
galleries.note: Capitol Hill's social heart for emerging and BIPOC artists; exhibitions, readings and music in one hybrid room.

galleries.name: AMcE Creative Arts
galleries.note: Recent arrival with an ambitious contemporary program and fair aspirations, signalling new commercial energy on Capitol Hill.

galleries.name: Martyr Sauce
galleries.note: Tariqa Waters's pop-art project space and micro-museum; playful, irreverent, and a visible platform for Black artists in Pioneer Square.

galleries.name: Veronica
galleries.note: Artist-organized space showing sharp, research-driven work by younger regional and out-of-town artists.

galleries.name: Specialist
galleries.note: Small artist-run venue with a conceptually rigorous, quickly rotating program that critics follow closely.

galleries.name: G. Gibson Gallery
galleries.note: Gail Gibson's gallery was for thirty years the Northwest's most serious photography dealer; now operating privately after closing its public space.

galleries.name: Roq La Rue Gallery
galleries.note: Kirsten Anderson's gallery put Seattle at the centre of pop surrealism from 1998; closed its storefront in 2021 but shaped a whole scene.

galleries.name: Zinc Contemporary
galleries.note: Clean-lined contemporary program of abstraction and photo-based work by Northwest and national artists.

galleries.name: Shift Gallery
galleries.note: Artist-run cooperative offering members annual solos; a steady incubator within the Tashiro Kaplan arts building.

galleries.name: Core Gallery
galleries.note: Member-run space with a well-regarded juried solo program for emerging artists.

galleries.name: Push/Pull
galleries.note: Artist-run gallery, shop and studio for comics, illustration and zine culture; the hub of Seattle's alt-comics community.

galleries.name: Vestibule
galleries.note: Curator-run Ballard project space known for tightly conceived group shows and support of experimental practice.

galleries.name: Bonfire Gallery
galleries.note: Historic Nihonmachi storefront showing contemporary painting, ceramics and Asian-American artists.

galleries.name: Flatcolor Gallery
galleries.note: Long-standing home for street art, graffiti and lowbrow practice in Seattle, with international guest artists.

galleries.name: Treason Gallery
galleries.note: Contemporary and urban-art gallery with a strong secondary-market and editions component.

galleries.name: Ltd. Art Gallery
galleries.note: Pop-culture and illustration gallery with themed group shows that draw large young audiences.

galleries.name: Ghost Gallery
galleries.note: Tiny, densely hung salon of small-format work by dozens of local artists; a long-lived Capitol Hill fixture.

galleries.name: Slip Gallery
galleries.note: Georgetown artist-run space for installation and experimental exhibitions outside the commercial circuit.

galleries.name: Fogue Gallery
galleries.note: Georgetown gallery and studios showing a broad cross-section of Seattle artists; anchor of the neighborhood art walk.

galleries.name: Equinox Studios
galleries.note: Vast industrial complex of artist and maker studios whose open-house exhibitions are among the city's largest public art events.

galleries.name: Base: Experimental Arts + Space
galleries.note: Platform for performance, sound and time-based practice that commercial galleries rarely accommodate.

galleries.name: Interstitial
galleries.note: Influential Georgetown space for video, new media and installation in the late 2010s; shaped local expectations for time-based art.

galleries.name: Mount Analogue
galleries.note: Publishing-and-exhibition project blending poetry, performance and visual art; nomadic since leaving its storefront but critically visible.

galleries.name: Vignettes
galleries.note: Sierra Stinson's apartment-gallery series that gave first shows to many now-established Seattle artists.

galleries.name: Cairo
galleries.note: DIY gallery, shop and music venue that defined a strand of 2010s Capitol Hill youth culture and artist community.

galleries.name: The Alice
galleries.note: Georgetown artist-run gallery praised for rigorous, curatorially framed exhibitions during its run.

galleries.name: Season
galleries.note: Robert Yoder's by-appointment gallery, admired for pairing Seattle artists with sympathetic national figures.

galleries.name: SAM Gallery
galleries.note: Rental-and-sales gallery presenting Northwest contemporary artists to a broad museum audience; a longstanding first market for many locals.

galleries.name: Jack Straw New Media Gallery
galleries.note: Rare dedicated venue for sound art and audio-based installation, tied to a respected artist-residency program.

galleries.name: Hedreen Gallery
galleries.note: Seattle University's exhibition space, known for socially engaged curatorial projects and collaborations with local artist-organizers.

galleries.name: ArtsWest Gallery
galleries.note: West Seattle's principal contemporary gallery, programmed in dialogue with the theatre's season.

galleries.name: Youngstown Cultural Arts Center
galleries.note: Delridge arts centre whose galleries and studios foreground youth, immigrant and community-based artists.

galleries.name: LANGSTON (Langston Hughes Performing Arts Institute)
galleries.note: Black arts institution in the Central District whose visual-art exhibitions and residencies complement its performance program.

galleries.name: INSCAPE Arts
galleries.note: Former immigration detention building converted into 125 artist studios with regular public open-studio exhibitions.

galleries.name: yəhaw̓ Indigenous Creatives Collective
galleries.note: Grew from a landmark 200-artist exhibition into an ongoing Indigenous-led organization with studio and gallery space and public commissions.

galleries.name: Onyx Fine Arts Collective
galleries.note: Artist collective mounting large annual surveys of Black Northwest artists in borrowed and partner venues.

galleries.name: Bherd Studios Gallery
galleries.note: Studio-and-gallery complex north of downtown known for its annual small-works show and support of illustrators and muralists.

galleries.name: Phinney Center Gallery
galleries.note: Neighborhood association gallery with a juried program that has shown north-end artists for decades.

galleries.name: KOBO at Higo
galleries.note: Japanese craft-and-art gallery in the historic Higo store, mixing contemporary ceramics and design with neighborhood history exhibits.

galleries.name: Vetri Glass
galleries.note: Traver's separate downtown storefront for emerging glass artists and small-scale contemporary work.

galleries.name: Western Bridge
galleries.note: Bill and Ruth True's 2004–2012 exhibition space for their international collection; the most ambitious private contemporary venue Seattle has had.

galleries.name: Suyama Space
galleries.note: Architect George Suyama's timber-framed hall commissioned major site-specific installations for twenty years until 2017; a benchmark for installation art in the city.

galleries.name: Lawrimore Project
galleries.note: Scott Lawrimore's 2006–2012 gallery was the most conceptually daring commercial space of its era and reshaped what Seattle dealers attempt.

galleries.name: Platform Gallery
galleries.note: Championed emerging Northwest artists in the 2000s and helped export them to national fairs before closing.

galleries.name: Howard House
galleries.note: Billy Howard's gallery (1998–2011) built the careers of numerous regional contemporary artists and set a professional standard for the market.

galleries.name: Francine Seders Gallery
galleries.note: From 1966 to 2013 the dealer for Jacob Lawrence, Gwendolyn Knight and Michael Spafford; arguably the most historically important gallery in Seattle's history.
